title: Seroquel and Alcohol: Risks, Sleep Doses, and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on Seroquel (quetiapine)? How the two stack sedation and drop blood pressure, what it means for low sleep doses, timing, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Seroquel (quetiapine)? How alcohol stacks with its sedation, what low sleep doses mean, timing tips, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Seroquel (quetiapine) and alcohol are a poor mix, and the drug's prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol while taking it. Both slow down your brain, both can make you dizzy or faint when you stand up, and quetiapine is strongly sedating on its own. Stack the two and you can end up far sleepier, clumsier, and more confused than you expect, with a real risk of falls, accidents, choking on vomit while deeply asleep, and, at higher amounts, dangerously slowed breathing. Alcohol also works against the reasons people take quetiapine in the first place: it destabilizes mood, worsens depression, and wrecks the second half of the night's sleep. This guide explains how the interaction works, what it means if you take a small dose for sleep, how timing works if you've already been drinking, and the warning signs that need help right away.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on a day you take Seroquel unless your prescriber has told you specifically what is okay for you. If you've been drinking and your dose is due, don't take it on top of the alcohol without checking with your prescriber or pharmacist first, and never double up later to make up for a missed dose. Never use alcohol to make quetiapine "work better" for sleep. Don't stop quetiapine suddenly so you can drink, either. If someone who mixed the two is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, fainting, or confused, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your quetiapine and knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if** you take quetiapine and drink at all, you want to know whether any amount of alcohol is okay for you, you take other sedating medicines (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioid painkillers, antihistamines, muscle relaxants, gabapentin), or you've noticed your drinking creeping up since starting it. **Get emergency help (call 911) if** someone who mixed quetiapine and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, has a racing or irregular heartbeat, or has a seizure. **If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) any time, day or night. Outside the US, contact your local emergency number or crisis line.

## What Seroquel Is and Why People Take It

Seroquel is the brand name for **quetiapine**, a prescription medicine in the class called atypical (or second-generation) antipsychotics. It was first approved by the FDA in 1997. An extended-release version, Seroquel XR, came later. Today most people take a generic.

The name "antipsychotic" puts some people off, but quetiapine is used for a wider range of conditions than the label suggests:

- **Schizophrenia**, its original approved use.
- **Bipolar disorder**, for manic episodes, for depressive episodes, and to help prevent relapse alongside a mood stabilizer.
- **Major depression**, where the extended-release form is approved as an add-on when an antidepressant alone hasn't been enough.
- **Off-label uses**, most commonly insomnia and anxiety, usually at low doses.

That last point matters for this article. A large number of people who take quetiapine aren't taking it for psychosis at all. They take 25 or 50 mg at night because it helps them sleep. Those people often assume a small "sleep dose" can't interact much with a couple of drinks. As you'll see below, the sedating part of quetiapine is exactly the part that's strongest at low doses, so that assumption doesn't hold up well.

## How Seroquel and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Quetiapine and alcohol don't mainly clash in the liver the way some drug combinations do. Quetiapine is broken down mostly by a liver enzyme called CYP3A4, and alcohol doesn't have a big effect on that pathway. The problem is what the two do to your brain and blood pressure once they're both on board.

### 1. Stacked sedation

Quetiapine blocks several kinds of receptors in the brain. One of them, the **histamine H1 receptor**, is the same target that makes old-fashioned allergy pills like Benadryl so drowsy. Quetiapine binds to it very strongly, and that effect is already in full swing at low doses. That's why it knocks people out.

Alcohol is a sedative too. It boosts GABA, the brain's main "slow down" signal, and dampens glutamate, its main "go" signal. When you combine a strong antihistamine-style sedative with alcohol, the effects add together. You get heavier drowsiness, slower reactions, poorer coordination, and fuzzier judgment than either one would cause alone.

At higher amounts of either, this can slow breathing, which is the most dangerous part of mixing any sedatives. It's also why passing out after drinking on quetiapine is riskier than it sounds. Someone who is deeply sedated may not wake up properly if they vomit or if their breathing becomes obstructed.

### 2. Blood pressure drops when you stand

Quetiapine also blocks **alpha-1 adrenergic receptors**, which help your blood vessels tighten when you stand up. Blocking them can cause **orthostatic hypotension**: a sudden drop in blood pressure when you get up, which feels like dizziness, lightheadedness, a greyed-out vision, or fainting. The label warns about this, especially in the first days of treatment and after a dose increase.

Alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you, which pushes blood pressure in the same direction. Put the two together and that late-night trip to the bathroom becomes a real fall risk. Falls are one of the most common ways this combination causes harm, particularly in older adults.

### 3. Thinking, judgment, and memory

The prescribing information cautions that quetiapine can impair judgment, thinking, and motor skills, and tells people not to drive or operate machinery until they know how it affects them. Alcohol does all of the same things. Together they make blackouts, bad decisions, and accidents more likely, and they can make it harder to notice how impaired you actually are.

### 4. Heart rhythm

Quetiapine can lengthen a measure of the heart's electrical cycle called the **QT interval**, and the label lists this as a risk to keep in mind, particularly in overdose or alongside other drugs that do the same. Heavy drinking, especially when it leads to vomiting and low potassium or magnesium, can make the heart more prone to rhythm problems. For most people taking a normal dose this isn't the main concern, but it's one reason a racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat after mixing the two shouldn't be brushed off.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Actually Say

The US prescribing information for Seroquel is direct about this. In its patient counseling section, it tells patients to **avoid consuming alcoholic beverages** while taking the drug. It also notes that because quetiapine acts mainly on the central nervous system, caution is needed when combining it with other centrally acting drugs and alcohol.

The label also reports that in a clinical trial, quetiapine made the effects of alcohol on thinking and movement stronger. That's the core finding, and it lines up with the mechanism above.

What you won't find is a safe number of drinks. There's no official threshold like "one drink is fine." Because quetiapine is used across a huge dose range (from 25 mg for sleep to 800 mg for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder), and because it's prescribed for conditions that alcohol itself can worsen, any advice about "how much" has to come from the person who prescribed it.

## Low-Dose Seroquel for Sleep and Alcohol

If you take a small dose of quetiapine at night for sleep, this is the section to read closely.

**The sleep dose is the sedating dose.** At 25 to 50 mg, quetiapine's main effect is that strong antihistamine-style drowsiness. Many of its other effects only appear at higher doses. So a low dose doesn't mean a low interaction with alcohol. If anything, the part of quetiapine that clashes most with alcohol is the part you're taking it for.

**Morning grogginess gets worse.** Plenty of people already wake up foggy on quetiapine, sometimes called a "Seroquel hangover." Alcohol adds its own hangover: dehydration, poor sleep in the second half of the night, headache, and low mood. Stacking the two can make the next morning rough and can leave you impaired for driving well into the day.

**Alcohol undoes the sleep benefit.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep, then fragments sleep later in the night as your body processes it. You get less REM sleep and more waking. Our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains that rebound effect in detail. Combining alcohol with a sleep medicine tends to give you a heavier crash early in the night without fixing the broken sleep later.

**Sleep guidelines don't favor quetiapine for insomnia anyway.** It's a common off-label choice, but sleep-medicine guidelines generally don't recommend it as a first-line insomnia treatment, partly because even low doses can bring weight gain, changes in blood sugar and cholesterol, and next-day sedation. If you take it for sleep and you also drink regularly, that's a good reason to talk to your prescriber about whether it's still the right fit. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the usual first-line recommendation. A similar trade-off applies to another common off-label sleep drug, covered in our [trazodone and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/trazodone-and-alcohol).

## Can You Drink on Seroquel at All? The "Just One Drink" Question

This is the question most people are actually asking, so here's a straight answer.

The label says to avoid alcohol, and that's the safest default. In practice, some prescribers will tell an individual patient on a stable dose that an occasional single drink is acceptable for them. That's a judgment based on their dose, their diagnosis, their other medicines, and how they react to quetiapine. It's not something you can safely work out on your own from a website.

If you're thinking about having a drink, these are the things that make it riskier:

- **You've just started quetiapine or recently changed your dose.** Dizziness and drowsiness are strongest in the first days and weeks.
- **You're on a higher dose**, for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or depression.
- **You take other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines like Xanax, sleep pills, opioids, gabapentin, muscle relaxants, or sedating antihistamines. Each one adds to the stack. Our [Xanax and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) covers why that particular combination is so dangerous.
- **You're older**, have low blood pressure, or have had falls.
- **You have sleep apnea**, since both quetiapine and alcohol can relax the airway and dampen breathing during sleep.
- **Your mood is unstable right now.** Alcohol can trigger mood episodes and makes impulsive behavior more likely.

If your prescriber has said an occasional drink is okay, ask them to be specific about how much, how often, and how it fits around your dose time. Then stick to that, drink slowly with food, and don't drive afterward.

## Timing: How Long After Seroquel Can You Drink, and Vice Versa?

There's no official waiting period, and quetiapine's timing makes the question harder than it sounds.

**How long it stays active.** Regular (immediate-release) quetiapine peaks in the blood roughly 1.5 hours after a dose and has a half-life of around 7 hours, meaning about half is cleared in that time. The extended-release form (Seroquel XR) peaks later, around 6 hours after a dose, and releases more slowly. Quetiapine is also turned into an active by-product (norquetiapine) that lingers longer. For people taking it daily, there is always some in the system.

That's the main reason "spacing it out" doesn't work well for regular users. If you take quetiapine every night, you aren't drinking at a time when there's no quetiapine in your body. You're drinking on top of a steady level of it.

**If you've already been drinking and your dose is due:**

- Don't take a higher dose or an extra dose to "sleep it off."
- Call your prescriber, a pharmacist, or an after-hours nurse line about whether to take tonight's dose. Many people are advised to skip a single dose rather than combine it with a significant amount of alcohol, but whether that's right depends on what you take it for. Skipping doses can matter more for some conditions, like bipolar disorder or schizophrenia, than for others.
- If you do skip a dose, don't double up the next night.
- Make sure someone knows you've been drinking and are on a sedating medicine, and get up slowly if you need the bathroom in the night.

**If you took your dose and then drank:** stop drinking, drink water, stay with someone if you feel very drowsy or dizzy, and don't drive. If any of the emergency signs below show up, call 911.

## Don't Stop Seroquel Just So You Can Drink

Some people skip quetiapine for a weekend so they can drink without worrying about the interaction. This backfires in a few ways.

Stopping quetiapine suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms, which the label describes as including insomnia, nausea, and vomiting. Those overlap with a hangover and can make the next few days much worse. More importantly, missing doses can let the condition it's treating come back. For bipolar disorder in particular, a gap in treatment combined with heavy drinking and lost sleep is a well-known recipe for a mood episode. If you want to stop or reduce quetiapine, plan it with your prescriber, who can taper the dose.

## Alcohol, Mood, and the Conditions Quetiapine Treats

Beyond the direct drug interaction, alcohol tends to make the underlying conditions harder to manage.

- **Depression.** Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant, and regular drinking is linked with lower mood and more anxiety in the days after. Our explainer on [whether alcohol is a depressant](/never-hungover/is-alcohol-a-depressant) walks through what that means. The "hangxiety" many people feel the day after drinking can be stronger in people already dealing with depression or anxiety.
- **Bipolar disorder.** Alcohol use is common in people with bipolar disorder and is associated with more frequent mood episodes, poorer response to treatment, and more impulsive behavior. Lost sleep from a night out can itself trigger mania in some people.
- **Psychosis.** Alcohol can worsen symptoms and makes it harder to stick to treatment.
- **Suicide risk.** Like antidepressants, quetiapine carries an FDA boxed warning about suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens, and young adults. Alcohol lowers inhibition and raises impulsivity, and mixing large amounts of alcohol with sedating medicines is a dangerous combination for anyone in a crisis. If you notice your mood dropping or thoughts of self-harm, call or text **988** in the US, or your local crisis line, right away.

If you take an antidepressant alongside quetiapine, which is common, see our [antidepressants and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol) for how that class interacts with drinking.

## Weight, Blood Sugar, and Cholesterol: The Slower Interaction

Quetiapine can raise appetite, weight, blood sugar, and blood fats such as triglycerides. That's why prescribers check weight and blood work over time. Alcohol pushes on some of the same levers. Drinks carry a lot of calories, late-night drinking tends to bring late-night eating, and heavy drinking can raise triglycerides and disrupt blood sugar control. If you have diabetes or prediabetes, alcohol can also cause low blood sugar hours later, and the sedation from quetiapine can make that harder to notice.

None of this is an emergency on a single night, but it's worth knowing that regular drinking can quietly make one of quetiapine's main long-term downsides worse.

## Heat, Dehydration, and Body Temperature

Antipsychotics, including quetiapine, can make it harder for your body to regulate its temperature, and the label advises care in situations like intense exercise, hot weather, and dehydration. Alcohol dehydrates you and impairs your sense of how hot or unwell you are. A long day of drinking outdoors in the heat, at a festival, or in a hot tub is a situation to be especially careful about on quetiapine. Drink water alongside anything alcoholic and get out of the heat if you feel faint, confused, or stop sweating.

## A Note on Quetiapine and Alcohol Withdrawal

You may see quetiapine mentioned in connection with drinking problems. It has been studied as a way to help people cut down on alcohol, with mixed results; at least one sizable placebo-controlled trial in very heavy drinkers did not find that it helped. It is not a standard treatment for alcohol withdrawal.

This matters for one practical reason. If someone who drinks heavily every day stops suddenly, they can develop withdrawal, which can include shaking, sweating, a racing heart, agitation, hallucinations, and seizures. That can be life-threatening. Don't try to manage it with leftover quetiapine or other sedatives. Get medical help, because doctors have safer, proven ways to manage it.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help Right Away

**Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has mixed quetiapine and alcohol:**

- Is very hard to wake, or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly, shallowly, or irregularly, or making gurgling or snoring sounds while unresponsive
- Faints, or collapses when standing
- Has a very fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat, or chest pain
- Has a seizure
- Is very confused, or has blue or grey lips or fingertips
- May have taken more quetiapine than prescribed

While you wait for help, don't leave them alone. If they're breathing but not fully awake, roll them onto their side (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit. Don't try to make them throw up, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower to "wake them up." Those don't reverse the sedation.

For questions about a possible overdose that isn't an emergency yet, you can call **Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222** in the US, any time.

**Call your prescriber soon (not an emergency) if:**

- You're regularly drowsy or dizzy the morning after drinking on quetiapine
- You've had a fall or a near-miss while driving
- You find yourself drinking more since starting it, or using alcohol to get to sleep
- Your mood has become less stable

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from the quetiapine-and-alcohol combination if you:

- Take other sedating medicines, especially benzodiazepines, opioids, sleep pills, or gabapentin
- Are over 65 (quetiapine also carries a boxed warning about higher death rates in older adults with dementia-related psychosis, for whom it isn't approved)
- Have low blood pressure, heart rhythm problems, or a history of fainting
- Have sleep apnea or a lung condition that affects breathing
- Have diabetes, or have been told your blood sugar or cholesterol is high
- Have liver disease, which can slow how fast quetiapine is cleared
- Have recently started quetiapine or changed your dose

For a wider look at how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## What About Hangover Supplements Like DHM?

If you're on quetiapine, the most important point is this: **talk to your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement that might affect the brain**, and that includes hangover products.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, and some of that research shows it acting on the brain's GABA-A receptors, the same system alcohol and many sedatives act on. There is no research on combining DHM with quetiapine, so nobody can tell you it's safe to stack them. There is also no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, fall risk, or breathing risk of mixing quetiapine with alcohol. It does not make drinking on quetiapine safe.

If you don't take quetiapine or other sedating medicines and you're simply looking for a way to feel better after an occasional night out, DHM is one option some people use. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. The habits with the best evidence behind them, though, are the unglamorous ones in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover): drink less, drink slower, eat, and alternate with water.

## The Bottom Line

- Seroquel's prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol. The two stack their sedation and both can drop your blood pressure when you stand.
- The main risks are heavy drowsiness, falls, accidents, impaired judgment, and, at higher amounts, slowed breathing.
- A low "sleep dose" is not a low-risk dose with alcohol. The sedating effect is strongest at exactly those doses.
- Spacing doses and drinks apart doesn't work well if you take quetiapine daily, because there's always some in your system.
- Don't stop quetiapine suddenly so you can drink, and don't take extra to sleep off alcohol.
- If your prescriber says an occasional drink is okay, get specifics and stick to them.
- Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or fainting after mixing the two. If you're struggling with your mood, call or text 988.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Seroquel?**

The Seroquel prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol. Quetiapine and alcohol both sedate the brain and both can lower blood pressure when you stand, so together they can cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness, falls, and impaired judgment, and at higher amounts slowed breathing. Some prescribers allow an occasional drink for a specific patient on a stable dose, but that's an individual decision. Ask the person who prescribed it before drinking at all.

**Is quetiapine the same as Seroquel?**

Yes. Quetiapine is the generic name of the drug, and Seroquel (and Seroquel XR for the extended-release form) is the brand name. The alcohol warning applies to every form, including generic immediate-release and extended-release quetiapine.

**Is it safe to drink if I only take a low dose of Seroquel for sleep?**

Not necessarily. At 25 to 50 mg, quetiapine's main effect is strong antihistamine-style sedation, which is the part that adds most directly to alcohol. A low dose can still cause heavy drowsiness, dizziness on standing, and morning grogginess when combined with alcohol. Alcohol also disrupts sleep later in the night, which works against the reason you're taking it. Talk to your prescriber before mixing them.

**How long after taking Seroquel can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Immediate-release quetiapine peaks about 1.5 hours after a dose with a half-life of around 7 hours, and the extended-release form peaks later and releases more slowly. If you take it every day, there's always some in your system, so spacing it out doesn't remove the interaction. Ask your prescriber what's safe for your dose and schedule.

**Should I skip my Seroquel dose if I've been drinking?**

Don't take extra, and don't combine a dose with a significant amount of alcohol without advice. Call your prescriber, a pharmacist, or an after-hours nurse line, because whether skipping a single dose is right depends on why you take it. Missing doses matters more for conditions like bipolar disorder or schizophrenia. If you do skip one, don't double up the next time.

**What happens if you mix Seroquel and alcohol?**

Most often, much stronger drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and fuzzy thinking than either alone, plus a higher chance of fainting or falling when you stand up. With larger amounts, it can lead to deep sedation and slowed breathing, which is a medical emergency. Call 911 if someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, fainting, or has a seizure.

**Can I stop taking Seroquel for a weekend so I can drink?**

It's not a good idea. Stopping quetiapine suddenly can cause discontinuation symptoms such as insomnia, nausea, and vomiting, and missing doses can let the condition it treats come back, especially with the lost sleep that often comes with drinking. If you want to stop or reduce quetiapine, plan a taper with your prescriber.

**Can I take DHM or a hangover supplement while on Seroquel?**

Ask your prescriber or pharmacist first. DHM acts on GABA-A receptors in animal research, and there is no research on combining it with quetiapine. There is also no good evidence that DHM reduces the risks of mixing quetiapine and alcohol, so it does not make drinking on quetiapine safe.
